2426	# Fair play
2427	
2428	**Rules at a glance**
2429	
2430	You submit an agentic system: one agent or several. In the sandbox it does the whole job on its own: finds what it needs on the four websites, works out the bid and submits it. Nobody helps it during a run.
2431	
2432	**Not allowed**
2433	
2434	- **Hardcoding:** copying values from the websites into your package (prices, material numbers, totals, discounts, logins, TANs), including in prompts and notes, also as defaults or fallbacks. Using what the task brief tells every team, like the sales director's mailbox, is fine.
2435	- **Pre-solving:** working out the answer yourself, or having an AI assistant do it, and putting the result in your package. Exploring the sites with an assistant is fine.
2436	- **Scripts instead of agents:** a fixed click path, or a crawler that grabs everything for one model call. A model has to choose where to go, what to search for and what matters.
2437	- **Outside help during a run:** contacting anything besides our platform and the four websites, calling a model other than through our proxy (your own API keys work through it), running a model inside the sandbox, or starting your own browsers (use the up to 4 provided). Setup may install dependencies.
2438	
2439	**How it's checked:** an AI reviewer reads every submitted package before its scored run. Unclear cases are flagged and stay off the leaderboard until an organizer has looked. The final runs on websites and data your system hasn't seen.
2440	
2441	The details follow.
2442	
2443	## Allowed
2444	
2445	- Any agent design; the free hosted models, or any provider and model with your own key, through the proxy; any
2446	  amount of tokens.
2447	  The proxy forwards your calls unchanged and measures them: reported usage is metered at the published model
2448	  prices, and an upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. See [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls)
2449	  for SDK configuration.
2450	- Keeping your model key as a [team secret](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#team-secrets) rather than in your package.
2451	- Your own code, prompts and tools; open-source libraries installed during setup.
2452	- Using what you learned with the scouting logins and in test runs about how the websites work.
2453	- Up to 4 browsers at a time: ask for them with `"browsers"` in `agent.json` and use as many tabs and browser
2454	  contexts inside them as you like.
2455	
2456	## Not allowed
2457	
2458	- Hardcoding values copied from the public scenario or its websites into code, config, prompts or notes, including defaults and fallbacks: tender references, material numbers, prices, totals, discounts, logins and TANs. Facts the task brief states for every scenario, such as the sales director's mailbox, are
2459	  rules you may use.
2460	- A scripted solution. Your agent system must be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the
2461	  information and makes the decisions. Code can help it (browser control, parsing, arithmetic, checks, reading a
2462	  page or document the model chose, paging through results it asked for), and several agents and browsers may work
2463	  in parallel. Rejected: a fixed script that clicks through known pages with the model unused or only as a fallback,
2464	  and a crawler that collects the websites and hands everything to the model at the end.
2465	- Bundling or running a local model, or reaching any model other than through the proxy.
2466	- Contacting hosts other than the API and the challenge's websites, or trying to get data out of the sandbox.
2467	- Starting browsers of your own in the sandbox, headless ones included. At most 4 browsers run at a time: ask for up
2468	  to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts inside them freely, and don't start others.
2469	  On your own machine (developing with the scouting logins) your agent starts its own browsers; that is up to you.
2470	- Attacking the platform, the websites, the sandbox or other teams; sharing scored-run data.
2471	
2472	## How it is checked
2473	
2474	- **Package review before any scored run:** an AI code reviewer, a coding agent that reads your whole package in an
2475	  isolated VM. Outcomes: passed, flagged or rejected (no runs). A flagged package still runs and scores, but its
2476	  result stays off the public leaderboard and the activity feed until an organizer passes it; your team sees it
2477	  marked "flagged: waiting for an organizer". Notes and docs addressed to the reviewer are not evidence of compliance
2478	  and do not count against you on their own. Instructions trying to steer the reviewer's verdict do.
2479	  The reviewer's reasons stay with the organizers: your team reads "Flagged by the reviewing agent" or "Rejected by
2480	  the reviewing agent". Someone from Atira looks at flagged packages shortly and unflags a misdetection; if you think
2481	  a reject is one, contact the Atira team.
2482	- **The organizers decide flagged packages, and can look at any submission:** they pass it, add an internal note
2483	  (this changes nothing you or the leaderboard see) or disqualify it. A disqualified submission and its runs read
2484	  "disqualified": it leaves the leaderboard and the final run, its runs still going stop, and your team page shows the
2485	  organizers' reason.
2486	- **Hardcoded values:** the reviewer rejects copied scenario values in code or config, even in defaults or fallbacks.
2487	- **The final run** uses a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a
2488	  supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software,
2489	  with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently
2490	  across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it. That run weighs most when we pick the
2491	  winners, so build a system that works the answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
2492	- **The sandbox** reaches only our API and the websites, so every model call passes the proxy and is measured.
2493	  Your team secrets reach only the timed run step and are redacted from its logs.
2494	- **Website logins** exist only for a live run and stop working when it ends.
2495	- **Browsers:** the sandbox stops any browser your agent starts beyond the ones it asked for and notes it in the
2496	  run's logs: `[platform] stopped a browser the agent started`.
2497	- **Everything measured** (tokens, cost, time, the answer) is recorded by the platform, never reported by you.
2498	
2499	Breaking these rules gets the submission rejected before it runs, or removed later; repeated or deliberate attempts
2500	get the team disqualified.
2501	
2502	## Flagged results
2503	
2504	A flagged result stays off the public leaderboard until an organizer passes it. **Show flagged** on the leaderboard
2505	lists flagged results, without a rank.

2511	# Submitting
2512	
2513	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
2514	
2515	You submit your agent system as a gzipped tarball. We review it, run it once in the sandbox on the public dataset
2516	and score it. That run determines its rank on the leaderboard. When the hackathon ends, your latest submission that
2517	passed review runs once more, on a private dataset, in the [final run](#what-happens-next), which weighs most when we pick the winners.
2518	
2519	## Package layout
2520	
2521	```
2522	agent.json          {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": ["qwen"]}
2523	pyproject.toml      (or package.json, requirements.txt, ...)
2524	agent.py            your code
2525	```
2526	
2527	- `agent.json` at the root: `setup` (optional) and `run`, each an argv array. Both run in the package directory.
2528	  `browsers` (optional, 1 to 4, default 1) is how many browsers the sandbox starts for the run; see
2529	  [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#browsers). `models` (optional) lists the hosted models your agent system calls,
2530	  by provider id, all of them by default: the run's clock waits for those to warm up, and `[]` starts it right after
2531	  setup; see [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#scored-run).
2532	- At most 20 MB compressed; regular files only.
2533	- No secrets: the run gets everything it needs from the environment.
2534	
2535	## Upload
2536	
2537	```
2538	tar czf agent.tar.gz -C my-agent .
2539	curl --data-binary @agent.tar.gz \
2540	  -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/gzip" \
2541	  $API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions
2542	```
2543	
2544	The response (`202`) has your submission's id. Review is still pending and no runs exist yet: follow it with
2545	`GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions` for the review result and run ids, or watch the leaderboard.
2546	
2547	`$ATIRA_TOKEN` is your personal token: `atira login` signs the [CLI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md) in through the browser, and
2548	`atira token` prints the token (or sign in with plain curl, as the [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#signing-in) shows).
2549	
2550	Or let the CLI pack, check and upload the folder: `atira submit my-agent` (and `atira test-run my-agent` for a
2551	test run). It leaves out `.git`, `node_modules` and what `.gitignore` excludes. In a terminal, `submit` then opens
2552	your team page, which shows the review and links each scored run as it starts, and `test-run` opens the run page.
2553	
2554	## Test it in the sandbox first
2555	
2556	Upload the same tarball as a test run ("Test runs" on your team page, or
2557	`POST $API/v1/challenges/rfq/rehearsals` with the same headers). It runs once in the scored-run sandbox against
2558	the public scenario `public-1`, scored with the points for each part of the answer. Its live view shows the
2559	browser (a frame about every 1.5 s, or the live screen where available), the phases, every model call,
2560	and your logs as the agent prints them. Afterwards the recorded video stays available to
2561	your team. Up to 5 test runs at a time per team. `atira test-run my-agent` uploads it, starts the run
2562	and opens it live; `atira cancel` (or Cancel run on the run page) stops a run that has not finished, and frees its
2563	test-run slot at once.
2564	
2565	## Linking your GitHub repository
2566	
2567	The organizers ask each team to link the GitHub repository it builds its agent in, so they can review the
2568	code, for example to compare a winning submission with its source. On your team page, the captain chooses
2569	Connect a GitHub repository, installs the organizers' GitHub App on the account that owns the repository
2570	(granting it only that repository is enough), and picks the repository. Every member sees the linked repository,
2571	who linked it and when; the captain can switch or unlink it at any time.
2572	
2573	The app only reads the contents of the repositories you grant it; it cannot push, open issues or change
2574	settings. Linking does not change how you submit: scored submissions and test runs are still the tarballs
2575	described above. To withdraw access completely, unlink the repository and uninstall the app in your GitHub
2576	settings.
2577	
2578	## Watching your submission
2579	
2580	Each scored run has a live view with its phase, timer, model calls, tokens and cost. On the public dataset it also
2581	shows your team the browser (frames, and the live screen where available), the logs and errors
2582	unredacted and the scenario id, and the recording afterwards. The final run on the private dataset shows its
2583	screen, frames and recordings to the organizers only; your team reads its logs and errors with private values
2584	masked as `[private]`.
2585	
2586	## Resubmitting
2587	
2588	Submit as often as you like, one at a time: while a submission is still in review or has unfinished runs, the
2589	next upload is refused with `429`. Your **best complete** submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
2590	**latest** one that passed review goes into the final run. Your other submissions stay in your history at
2591	`$API/team`. Cancelling a submission's scored run ends that submission: it never completes, the leaderboard ignores it, and you
2592	can submit again.
2593	
2594	## What happens next
2595	
2596	1. **Review:** passed, flagged or rejected (no runs). A flagged submission still runs and scores, but its result
2597	   stays off the public leaderboard and the activity feed until an organizer passes it; your team sees it marked
2598	   "flagged: waiting for an organizer". Your team sees the outcome, not the reviewer's reasons. The organizers can
2599	   still pass or disqualify a submission later; a disqualified one reads "disqualified", leaves the leaderboard and
2600	   the final run, and your team page gives the organizers' reason.
2601	2. **Scored run:** one run in a fresh sandbox on the public dataset, setup first (up to 5 minutes, not counted),
2602	   then your run command (timed).
2603	3. **Ranking:** once the run has finished and review is passed, your submission appears on the leaderboard with its quality, cost and
2604	   time; ineligible answers rank after every eligible one.
2605	4. **Final run:** when the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review
2606	   (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected and disqualified ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it. It is the latest one, not the best one.
2607	   That run weighs most when we pick the winners ([Winners](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#winners)), so build a system that works the answer out from the websites, not one tuned to
2608	   the public scenario. Its results stay with the organizers until they publish them; then the leaderboard shows
2609	   the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", and the public-dataset board stays at
2610	   `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`.
2611	
2612	## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three
2613	
2614	The final runs your latest passed submission once, or up to three times if you opt in to **Best of 3** on your team
2615	page before the final starts (`atira final --best-of 3`). Your best attempt counts. Details:
2616	[Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#final-private-evaluation-one-attempt-or-best-of-three).

2643	## FAQ
2644	
2645	**Which models can I use?** The hosted models are free, and the starter kit shows how to call them. Or bring your own key for
2646	any provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Google, Groq, Mistral, DeepSeek, xAI, Together, Fireworks, or others the
2647	organizers add) and send its calls through the metering proxy. `GET /v1/runs/current` lists the proxy base URLs. Models must have a published
2648	price (a model too new for the platform's list counts at the price OpenRouter lists for it; OpenRouter reports its own)
2649	and satisfy any organizer model allowlist. See
2650	[the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls) for SDK setup.
2651	
2652	**Where do I keep my model key?** As a [team secret](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#team-secrets): the team page's Secrets list
2653	injects it into your agent's run step in test and scored runs, redacted from logs. Don't put keys in your
2654	package; we store packages and the review agent reads them.
2655	
2656	**Why does my model call get a 401?** "Add your OpenAI API key to the request" means no provider key arrived: set
2657	`OPENAI_API_KEY` (in test and scored runs, as a [team secret](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#team-secrets)). A 401 from the
2658	provider itself means the key is wrong. Check that `OPENAI_BASE_URL` points at the run's proxy
2659	(`$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1`, already set in test and scored runs); the same holds for any OpenAI-compatible provider.
2660	
2661	**How do my teammates and I sign in from a terminal?** Each person runs `atira login` on their own computer
2662	and approves it in the browser. Every device gets its own token; there is no shared team key to pass around.
2663	Without a browser on the machine, `atira login --device` prints a link and a code to approve elsewhere.
2664	
2665	**I lost a laptop, or a token leaked.** Revoke that device's token on your team page under Signed-in devices
2666	(`atira logout` revokes the one on the computer you are at). Leaving or being removed from a team ends your
2667	tokens' access to it at once.
2668	
2669	**My invite link says it is for someone else.** Invites are for one GitHub account. Sign in with the account
2670	the captain invited, or ask the captain to invite your GitHub username.
2671	
2672	**Does it cost me anything?** We charge nothing, and the models the platform hosts are free and never charged. If
2673	you bring your own key for another provider, that provider bills your key. The proxy measures every call and
2674	ranks you on its cost at the published prices; hosted calls count at simulated API prices.
2675	
2676	**How can I try my agent?** Develop locally against the public websites (`atira scout --env` exports the
2677	scouting logins), then test in the sandbox (`atira test-run ./my-agent`). A test run runs on `public-1`, the public
2678	RFQ scenario, and returns your score with the points for each part of the answer. With the scouting logins nothing
2679	counts: a bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
2680	
2681	**Is the public scenario's answer published?** No. The correct answer isn't published; your system has to work it
2682	out from the websites. Score breakdowns show the points for each part of the answer, never the expected values.
2683	
2684	**Which submission counts?** Your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard, which ranks scored runs on
2685	the public dataset. Your latest one that passed review (not your best one) goes into the final run: when the
2686	hackathon ends, the organizers run it once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it.
2687	That run weighs most when we pick the winners, ahead of your public score and the elegance of your system, so
2688	build an agent that works the answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario. See
2689	[Winners](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#winners).
2690	
2691	**Why did my answer get a 400?** It does not match `answer_schema`. The response lists the issues; the run is
2692	still open, so fix it and send it again.
2693	
2694	**Can I run my agent outside the sandbox?** While you develop, yes, anywhere, with the scouting logins. Test runs
2695	and scored runs always run in our sandbox.
2696	
2697	**Why is my run still queued?** Runs share the sandboxes in a fair order: scored runs first, then teams take turns,
2698	the team with the fewest runs in flight first. Your team runs up to 5 test runs at a time and can have up to 3
2699	waiting; the next waits while other teams' runs start. The run page says how many runs are ahead of yours, and
2700	`atira test-run --follow` prints it. See [the run queue](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#the-run-queue).
2701	
2702	**How do I stop a run?** `atira cancel <run>`, or Cancel run on its run page. The sandbox is removed, the run fails
2703	with "Cancelled by @you", and you can start the next test run at once. A cancelled scored run ends its
2704	submission: the leaderboard ignores it, and you can submit again.
2705	
2706	**Why do my requests get a 403 "Error 1010"?** The edge in front of our hosts refuses some default HTTP
2707	clients, such as Python's `urllib`. Send your own `User-Agent` header (the starter kit does).
2708	
2709	**Python says `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED` on my Mac.** Python from python.org ships without CA certificates.
2710	Run `Install Certificates.command` from its folder in Applications, or set `SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/cert.pem`.
2711	
2712	**What can my agent reach during a scored run?** Our API (including the model proxy) and the challenge's
2713	websites, nothing else. The `HTTP(S)_PROXY` variables in the run's environment route there; Python's
2714	`urllib`, `requests`, `httpx`, the Anthropic SDK and Node's `fetch` pick them up automatically. Chromium is
2715	already configured. Setup (`uv sync`, `npm ci`, …) has network, but nothing it starts survives into the
2716	run.
2717	
2718	## Event details
2719	
2720	- The event is on 10 October 2026.
2721	- A team has up to five people.
2722	- A scored run has 20 minutes on the clock; a test run has up to 2 hours.
2723	- Ask the organizers about the submission deadline and prizes.
2724	
2725	## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three
2726	
2727	The final runs your latest passed submission once, or up to three times if you opt in to **Best of 3** on your team
2728	page before the final starts (`atira final --best-of 3`). Your best attempt counts. Details:
2729	[Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#final-private-evaluation-one-attempt-or-best-of-three).

2	
3	You work in sales engineering for Linden Hydraulik und Komponenten GmbH, a German hydraulics and components manufacturer. Prepare one net EUR bid for Stadt Buchenstadt, Verkehrsbetriebe: Lieferung von Hydraulikzylinder für Werkstatt-Hebeanlagen (VG-2027-7093). The scenario date is 2027-01-25T09:00:00Z; the tender deadline is 2027-02-12T11:00:00Z.
4	
5	Collect the tender and its clarifications from the tender portal (Vergabeportal, `tender-portal`), the technical specification from the buyer's supplier portal (Lieferantenportal, `customer-portal`), materials and prices from the internal ERP (`erp`), and discount approvals from the sales mailbox in the webmail (Werkpost, `mail`). The websites are in German; obsolete documents and unrelated records are present.
6	
7	## Rules
8	
9	1. Quantity: start with the original tender quantity. For each position, use the quantity in the latest dated clarification that changes that position, if any.
10	2. Requirement: use the requirement referenced by the position in the specification revision marked current. Superseded revisions do not apply.
11	3. Material: select an active ERP material whose bore, stroke, pressure, mounting and certification all exactly equal that requirement. Blocked materials do not qualify. If any position has no matching active material, submit no_bid.
12	4. Unit price: use the material's price condition valid on the scenario date, including both validity endpoints. Choose the scale with the highest minimum quantity no greater than the final quantity. Apply the approved discount to that scale price and round the resulting unit price half up to the nearest cent.
13	5. Discount: use the most recent message from the sales director (leitung@ followed by the bidder's mailbox domain) that approves a discount for this exact tender reference. Approvals for other references and messages from other senders do not apply. If there is no approval, use zero percent.
14	6. Lead time: use the delivery-from-stock lead time in weeks when stock covers the final quantity; otherwise use the production lead time in weeks.
15	7. Total: sum each final quantity multiplied by its rounded discounted unit price, then round the total net amount half up to the nearest cent.
16	8. Decision: submit bid with one entry per tender position, identified by its position number, and currency EUR. If any active matching material is missing, submit no_bid with no positions and a total of zero.
17	
18	
19	## Additional rules
20	
21	These refine rules 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 and 7 above. Every submitted quantity is in pieces.
22	
23	- Partial submission: full credit requires every position, but the bid form lets you explicitly omit unfinished positions (Position auslassen / Teilpunkte). They receive no position points; completed positions retain their independent credit. Review lists the omitted position numbers. You must still sign and submit a bid; saving alone is not scored. A missing active material still calls for no_bid for full correctness; omission is a way to submit incomplete work, not a replacement decision rule.
24	- Finding records: the specification/data sheet names a Kataloggruppe for each requirement. Search the ERP for that group, then compare candidate attributes. Empty or over-broad searches do not list the catalogue; narrow to at most 20 results. Mail search combines words with AND: use the tender reference plus a subject/topic. Read the appropriate inbox/archive results. Opened pages and selected result sets may be extracted by helpers. Sites and positions can be investigated in parallel; no shared request quota or mandatory site order applies.
25	- Agent requirement: a language model must choose navigation targets, searches and relevant documents from observations at runtime and make the important decisions. Helpers may extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms. They must not autonomously discover and traverse the websites to assemble the complete task evidence before model-directed investigation. Multiple agents and parallel browser sessions are allowed.
26	- Commercial clauses: a tender Q&A answer may assign a position to a Konditionsgruppe. Resolve that key in the latest Konditionsregeln message for the exact reference from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. Its prose determines whether discount applies to base only, base plus mass surcharge, or neither; setup fees are always excluded. A group overrides the default rule, even when two positions select the same material. The separately reported surcharge is always BEFORE any discount. Positions without a group use the default base-only rule. The order-level approved percentage and its threshold calculation do not change.
27	- Withdrawn answers: a tender Q&A answer may withdraw (zurückziehen) an earlier answer by its number. Ignore the withdrawn answer's quantity change; the latest remaining change applies, otherwise the tender quantity.
28	- Scoped amendments: after selecting the governing full specification revision, read the tender Q&A for technical amendments naming that revision and requirement. Apply only the named attributes; all others are inherited. The latest dated applicable amendment wins per attribute. Amendments to other revisions do not apply.
29	- Shared stock: sum final quantities of all positions selecting the same material. Stock must cover that entire sum for every such position to use stock delivery; otherwise all use production delivery. No partial stock allocation. Price scales remain per position, not per material sum.
30	- Conditional discount: the latest exact-reference director approval may require a minimum undiscounted net order value. Compute that value from final quantities and valid per-position scale prices before any discount and excluding mass surcharges and setup fees, rounded half up to cents. The threshold is inclusive. If it fails, use 0 %, without falling back to older approvals. For no_bid a conditional approval yields 0 %.
31	- Units: tender and Q&A quantities use the position's stated unit. Convert Satz using the governing specification's pieces per set. Price scales, inventory, allocation weights and bid quantities all use final pieces. Carton rounding affects packaging cost only, never the bid quantity.
32	- Pricing breakdown: base_unit_price, surcharge_per_unit, packaging_per_unit and rebate_total are optional and earn independent credit. All monetary answers are net EUR. Base, surcharge and packaging are per piece; rebate_total is the credit for the whole position. Enter 0.00 for a known zero; blank means unanswered. Do not feed rounded per-piece breakdowns back into the final formula.
33	- These calculation rules apply to both practice and private datasets. Missing calculation fields lose only their own points; signing an incomplete bid is supported.
34	- Technical derivation: for a requirement marked nutzbarer Weg, apply its scoped amendments first, then add twice the per-end reserve from the revision-specific Technikfreigabe. Match the resulting nominal stroke to the ERP. Do not change the other attributes.
35	- Authority and time: resolve each key from the latest record no later than the scenario date, for the EXACT tender reference. Authorized subjects/senders (local part + bidder mailbox domain): Technikfreigabe/technik, Verpackungstarife/logistik, Terminfreigabe/logistik, Devisenfixing/finanzen, Rüstpools/kalkulation, Projektbonus/finanzen. A newer record replaces the older one; a failed quantity condition does not revive it. Unrelated references and future-dated records never apply.
36	- Currency: the valid condition names its currency and FX key. Normalize its price unit, select the per-position quantity scale, then convert with EUR per currency unit and HALF_UP to cents. This converted base_unit_price is used in all subsequent calculations and approval thresholds.
37	- Packaging: Q&A assigns the tariff key; ERP gives pieces per carton. Charge ceil(final pieces / carton size) cartons independently per position. Do not increase the bid quantity. Report packaging_per_unit in EUR, rounded HALF_UP; do not discount packaging.
38	- Delivery: Q&A assigns a commitment key. Apply it only if its material matches and pooled final demand for that material is within its inclusive ceiling. Otherwise use shared-stock delivery. A commitment may differ by position even for the same material.
39	- Shared setup: Q&A identifies pool members; ERP gives allocation mass (distinct from surcharge mass); the Rüstpools mail gives the one pool fee. Allocate by quantity × allocation mass using the cent-allocation rule in that mail. Add each allocation to that position's ordinary setup fee. Report surcharge_per_unit BEFORE discount, excluding packaging and bonus.
40	- Project bonus: the finance mail gives marginal percentage bands. Compute the eligible undiscounted EUR goods total, apply each band only to its portion, round the aggregate credit HALF_UP to cents, then allocate proportionally to eligible line goods values using largest remainders in cents (ties: ascending position identifier). Report rebate_total as the allocated EUR CREDIT FOR THE ENTIRE POSITION, not per piece; enter zero for nonmembers. This bonus is independent of discount clauses.
41	- Final price: clause-discounted EUR base + clause-discounted mass surcharge + (ordinary setup + allocated shared setup + carton cost − allocated project bonus) / final piece quantity. Use unrounded per-piece components and round HALF_UP once at the end. Sum quantity × rounded final unit price for total_net. Rounded breakdown fields are reports, not inputs to that final formula.
42	- Metal indices: select the latest exact-reference Preisindizes message from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. If the code lists validity windows, use the rate whose inclusive window contains the scenario date, not the last rate listed.
43	- Scoring in bid cases: decision 5, reference 5, discount 5, positions 75 minus any additional checks, correct total 5, arithmetic consistency 5.     base=site["url"]
    def get(p,data=None):
        try:
            r=op.open(urllib.parse.urljoin(base,p), data=urllib.parse.urlencode(data).encode() if data else None, timeout=30)
            return r.status, r.geturl(), r.read().decode("utf-8","replace")

## What is WebMCP?

WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) is a browser-native JavaScript API that lets websites expose structured, callable tools to AI agents operating inside a user's active browser session.

## Current API Status

The API moved from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext mid-2026, Chrome is running an origin trial through version 156, and almost every tutorial online still shows the deprecated call. WebMCP is currently in experimental stage, and early discussions may have referenced navigator.modelContext, but Chrome documentation now uses document.modelContext.

## Standardization Status

It is a W3C Draft Community Group Report (last published 26 August 2026), not a ratified standard. It is developed in the W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group, edited by engineers from Google and Microsoft.

## Browser Support

Chrome runs a public origin trial from version 149 through 156. Edge is behind a flag. Firefox and Safari have not committed.

## How It Works

WebMCP is a proposed web API that lets a page hand its own functions to an AI agent running in the browser. You call registerTool() and the agent can now invoke that JavaScript function.

input.content:
# Architecture options for the RFQ agent

Research note, 10 Oct 2026. Sources: the platform docs (`/start.md`, `/challenges/rfq.md`, `/llms-full.txt`), the
public run brief (`GET /v1/challenges/rfq/scouting`), and a light look at how the four scouting sites behave. No
scenario value (reference, material, price, login, label) is recorded here, and none may enter `agent/`.

## 1. What the problem statement actually asks for

One signed bid for one tender, assembled from four German business sites, entered in the tender portal's
configurator and signed with a TAN from the webmail. The answer goes in **on the site**, not through the API.

| Fact | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Order: eligible, then quality 0 to 100, then cost x time | Cost and time are only a tie-break. Correctness is the game. |
| Eligible = right tender reference in a **signed** submission | A run that never signs scores 0. Signing reliably is step one. |
| Exactly one submission, it ends the run | No "submit early, improve later". The agent needs a deadline-driven best answer. |
| 20 min scored run, TAN valid 5 min, going back clears later steps | Form entry is a transaction: have all values ready before starting it. |
| Money compared to the cent, 29 rules define one answer | Arithmetic must be deterministic code (Decimal, HALF_UP), never model output. |
| Final run = our **latest passed** submission on a private set | Every `atira submit` replaces the finalist. A worse later submit is a real loss. |
| Private set: same jobs, rules and schema; other software, layout, navigation, site names, data, and a different split of information across sites | Anything keyed on URL, selector, label, siteId or click order is worth zero there. |
| AI reviewer rejects fixed click paths, crawlers, copied values | The model must pick targets, searches and documents. Helpers may parse, paginate, calculate, validate, retry, fill. |
| Leaderboard today: best 21.5, most teams 0 or ineligible | Nobody has it. A correct, signed, partially right bid already ranks near the top. |

What stays constant between public and private, and is therefore safe to build on:

- the 29 rules and the scoring weights (the brief restates them in every run);
- the answer schema;
- the four job roles (tender portal, supplier portal, ERP, webmail) and the German domain vocabulary of the rules;
- the adversarial style: cookie walls, flaky error pages that need a retry, session timeouts, look-alike and
  superseded records, iframes and ZIPs, self-closing popups, paging, mixed time zones.

What does not stay constant: everything about how a site is built and where a fact lives.

Observed site behaviour that matters for design (behaviour, not content):

- Server-rendered pages, small (roughly 1 to 2 k characters of visible text). Reading as text is cheap.
- Identifiers are rendered with invisible characters between the letters, so naive string matching and regexes on
  page text fail. Text must be normalised; a screenshot is unaffected.
- Decoy UI drawn inside the page (fake browser bars, download prompts, notices). A text dump mixes it with content.
- At least one pointer-drag "unlock" widget. HTTP-only access cannot pass it; real pointer events are needed.
- Message bodies sit in lazy iframes; some content is behind a dialog or an explicit "request access" step.
- Random 503 pages with a retry link; each site reports times in a different zone.

So the task is four problems, not one: **(a)** find evidence on hostile sites, **(b)** decide which of several
competing records governs (exact reference, authorised sender, latest date not after the scenario date),
**(c)** exact arithmetic, **(d)** a long stateful form with a second-factor step. Browsing frameworks only address
(a) and (d). Most of the 100 points are lost in (b) and (c).

## 2. Overfit, underfit, and where the line is

- **Overfit** (dies on the private set, and the reviewer rejects it): selectors, URL paths, page labels, transaction
  codes, click sequences, `if site_id == ...`, prompt text that describes the public sites, few-shot examples copied
  from them, tuning until public-1 scores well.
- **Underfit** (what most of the leaderboard is doing): a generic "browse and figure it out" agent with no domain
  structure. It gets lost, burns the 20 minutes, and does arithmetic in its head.
- **Target: domain-typed, site-agnostic.** Encode what the rules guarantee (evidence schema, authority and time
  resolution, the calculator, the answer schema). Leave everything about the sites to the model at run time.

Rule of thumb for any line of code or prompt: *would it still be true on a site we have never seen?* The rules pass
that test. A label seen on public-1 does not, unless the brief itself states it (then read it from the brief at run
time rather than typing it into code).

## 3. The design space (axes)

Every web agent in use today is one choice per axis. "All combinations" is this table.

### A. What the model sees

| # | Option | Used by | Fit here |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A1 | Cleaned text / markdown of the page | reader tools, most RAG scrapers | Cheap, exact digits. Polluted by decoys and invisible characters; needs normalising. |
| A2 | Accessibility tree with element refs | Playwright MCP, browser-use, Comet | Good default: compact, actionable. Depends on site markup quality. |
| A3 | Screenshot only | Claude computer use, OpenAI CUA, Gemini computer use, UI-TARS | Immune to DOM tricks, handles drag widgets. Slow, costly, risky for cent-exact numbers. |
| A4 | Screenshot with numbered marks (Set-of-Marks) | WebVoyager, SeeAct | Middle ground; grounding is easier than raw coordinates. |
| A5 | **Hybrid: text first, screenshot on demand or when stuck** | Stagehand, Comet, most 2026 production agents | Best fit. Text for reading numbers, pixels for layout, decoys and widgets. |
| A6 | Network level: HTML or JSON over the browser's own session | "API-first" agents | Fast for reading. Cannot do pointer widgets; looks like a crawler if code picks the URLs. |
| A7 | Document parsers (PDF, ZIP, iframe) | everywhere | Required helper, explicitly allowed for a document the model chose. |

### B. How the model acts

| # | Option | Used by | Fit here |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B1 | Fixed primitive tools: click(ref), type, select, goto, back | browser-use, Playwright MCP | Reliable, many small steps, each one a model call. |
| B2 | Mouse and keyboard at coordinates | computer-use models | Needed only for pointer widgets and native dialogs. |
| B3 | Natural-language atomic actions with self-healing: act / extract / observe | Stagehand | Good ergonomics; one extra model call per action. |
| B4 | **Code as action**: the model writes a short Playwright snippet that runs in a guarded REPL | Webwright (MSR), CodeAct, smolagents | Several steps per model call, loops over rows for free. Strong on long tasks. |
| B5 | HTTP as action: the model issues a GET or a form POST through the browser context | hybrid API/browse agents | Fast reads on server-rendered sites; brittle on anything stateful. |
| B6 | Semantic tools built generically on B1: search(query), open(result), read_document(link), fill_form(mapping) | most in-house agents | Fewer steps, still site-agnostic if implemented from the live DOM, not from known selectors. |
| B7 | Site-declared tools (WebMCP, OpenAPI, llms.txt) | emerging | Not offered by these sites. Cheap to probe for; see section 8. |

### C. Who decides (control)

| # | Option | Used by | Fit here |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C1 | One ReAct loop | baseline everywhere | Context fills up, serial, slow. The 0 to 21 point results look like this. |
| C2 | Planner then executor | Agent-E, plan-and-act | Good, but the plan must change as Q&A reveals new keys. |
| C3 | **Lead plus parallel workers, each with its own context and browser** | Magentic-One, Anthropic's research pattern | Natural fit for 4 browsers. Workers return findings, not transcripts. |
| C4 | **Shared evidence ledger (blackboard)** | Magentic-One ledgers | Needed: tender Q&A yields keys that the mail and ERP searches depend on. |
| C5 | Staged graph with agentic stages | LangGraph-style | Good outer skeleton: discover, gather, resolve, calculate, enter, sign. |
| C6 | Redundant workers plus voting | self-consistency, debate | Nearly free in wall-clock with 32 concurrent Qwen calls. Use on high-value facts. |
| C7 | Independent verifier | generator plus critic | High value: every fact used is re-checked against its quoted source. |
| C8 | **Skill induction inside the run**: the model works one item by hand, then writes its own routine for the rest | Agent Workflow Memory, SkillWeaver, Voyager | Script speed without a shipped script. Generalises because the routine is authored against the site it finds. |
| C9 | Tree search with backtracking | LATS | Too slow, and form steps are not reversible. Read-only exploration at most. |

### D. Who computes

| # | Option | Fit here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D1 | Model does the arithmetic | No. Rounding order alone guarantees cent errors. |
| D2 | **Model extracts typed facts, deterministic code calculates** | Yes. The rules are fixed for both datasets, so this is the most general asset we can build. |
| D3 | Model turns rule prose into parameters (which clause, which allocation rule) | Needed where a mail states the rule in prose. Output is an enum or a small structured spec, then D2 runs it. |
| D4 | Model writes calculation code per run | Fallback for a rule variant D2 does not cover. |

### E. Which model does what

| # | Mix | Cost per run (rough) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| E1 | Qwen for everything | about $0.1 to 0.5 | No key needed. 256k context, tools, vision. Weakest link is multi-rule reasoning; D2 and C7 take that load off it. |
| E2 | Qwen workers, **Clef as gate** | adds cents | Clef returns calibrated probabilities for typed questions: "is this the current revision", "does this mail name exactly this reference", "which of these links". Good as verifier and as an abstain signal. Not a reader or planner. |
| E3 | Qwen workers, frontier lead and auditor (own key) | dollars | A handful of frontier calls for the plan, conflict resolution and the final audit. Best quality per dollar if we have a key. |
| E4 | Frontier everywhere | several dollars or more | Highest ceiling, slowest to tie-break. Only sensible because quality outranks cost. |
| E5 | Qwen for reading, a computer-use model for pointer widgets | small | Only if Qwen's own grounding fails on drag widgets. Test Qwen first; it is strong on GUI benchmarks. |
| E6 | Qwen x3 voting, disagreement escalates to Clef or frontier | small | Turns free concurrency into accuracy. |

Cost is a tie-break behind quality, so a mix should be chosen for correctness and variance first.

## 4. Named combinations

| # | Combination | Generalises | Quality ceiling | Time | Review risk | Build effort |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | browser-use or Stagehand loop, one model (A2, B1/B3, C1, D1) | Medium | Low | Slow | None | Lowest |
| 2 | Pure computer use, frontier model (A3, B2, C1, D1) | High for navigation | Low to medium | Slowest | None | Low |
| 3 | Fixed pipeline with scripted paths, model for extraction only | None | High on public only | Fast | **Rejected** | Medium |
| 4 | HTTP crawl of all sites, then one large model call | Low | Medium | Fast | **Rejected** (crawler) | Low |
| 5 | Lead plus 4 site workers, shared ledger, deterministic calculator (A5, B1+B6, C3+C4+C5, D2) | High | High | Medium | None | Medium |
| 6 | Combination 5 with code-as-action and in-run skill induction (B4, C8) | High | High | Fast | Low, if the model authors the code at run time | Medium to high |
| 7 | Combination 5 or 6 with voting and an independent verifier (C6, C7, Clef gate) | High | Highest | Medium | None | Higher |
| 8 | Combination 7 with a frontier lead and auditor (E3) | High | Highest | Medium | None | Same, needs a key |

Combinations 1 and 2 are where the field is, and why scores are low. 3 and 4 are the tempting shortcuts that the
rules exist to stop, and both fail on the private set anyway.

## 5. Recommendation

Build **5 first, grow it into 7**, on Qwen with Clef as a gate (E2 then E6). Add 6 (code as action) only after 5
signs a bid end to end. Move to 8 only if a frontier key is available and test runs show the remaining errors are
reasoning errors rather than retrieval errors.

```
brief ──> Lead (reads rules, writes the fact plan, owns the clock)
             │  questions                        ▲  typed findings + source quote
   ┌─────────┼─────────┬─────────┐               │
 Worker    Worker    Worker    Worker     one per browser; role found by looking, not by siteId
   └─────────┴────┬────┴─────────┘
            Evidence ledger   {key, value, unit, reference, sender, date, source, quote}
                  │
            Resolver (code)   exact reference, authorised sender, latest date <= scenario date
                  │
            Calculator (code) Decimal, HALF_UP at the steps the rules name, self-checking
                  │
            Verifier          re-reads each used fact against its quote; Clef or second pass
                  │
            Submitter         generic form agent: fill, TAN, review, sign; starts at a fixed time budget
```

Why this shape generalises:

- The only fixed knowledge is the rules. Workers get a **question** ("which price condition is valid on this date
  for this material, with all scales"), never a path.
- Site roles are discovered: each worker opens its site and reports what it holds. If the private set moves a fact
  to another site, the lead re-routes the question. Nothing branches on a site name.
- The model selects records; code only applies the tie-break the rule states. That split is exactly what the
  fair-play rules allow ("calculate, validate"), and it removes the most common reasoning error.
- One generic form filler serves any configurator: read the live form, map answer fields to inputs, write, re-read,
  confirm. German number formatting is a formatter, not a prompt instruction.

Build order, by points and by how well each step transfers:

1. **Signed submission with the right reference and decision.** Eligibility plus 10 points, and it beats most of the
   board. Includes the TAN flow and the deadline guard (begin entry with a fixed margin, submit by about T minus 90 s,
   use "omit position" for anything unfinished).
2. **Material and quantity per position** (35 % of position points): current revision, scoped amendments, Q&A
   quantity changes and withdrawals, unit conversion, exact attribute match, the no-bid decision.
3. **Base price, discount, lead time, total**: validity window, scale, currency, conditional approval, pooled stock.
4. **Surcharge, packaging, bonus, setup pool, metal index**: each is independent credit; add one at a time.

## 6. Measuring generalisation with one public scenario

We cannot see the private set, so we manufacture distribution shift locally.

- **Blind roles:** in local runs, shuffle site order and replace every `siteId` with an opaque token.
- **Perturbed sites:** a Playwright route handler that rewrites the public pages on the fly: renamed labels and
  navigation, reordered DOM, different CSS, moved links. Same data, different site. The score must not move.
- **Synthetic scenarios for the calculator:** generated inputs with hand-derived expected outputs, kept outside
  `agent/`. Property tests for rounding order, largest-remainder allocation, inclusive bounds, pooled stock.
- **Overfit lint:** a script that collects every distinctive token from the scouted pages and fails if any appears in
  `agent/` (code, prompts, config), unless the brief also states it.
- **Variance:** run the same package several times. A design that scores 60, 20, 60 is worse for a single final run
  than one that scores 50 every time. Decide on best-of-3 for the final from this number.
- **Fix classes, not instances:** when a test run loses points, the fix must be expressible without naming anything
  from public-1. If it cannot be, it is overfitting.
- **Submit discipline:** only submit a package that is at least as general as the current finalist, since the latest
  passed one is what runs on the private set.

## 7. Current state of `main`

- `main` holds the untouched starter kit (`solve()` returns `None`) plus `CLAUDE.md`.
- `CLAUDE.md` refers to `docs/plan.md`, `dev/smoke.py` and harness modules (`llm.py`, `extract.py`,
  `browser_tools.py`, `worker.py`, `tracing.py`). None of them are in the repository, on any remote branch.
- `agent.json` has no `browsers` key, so a run gets one browser.
- The team has two scored submissions, both ineligible with quality 0.

## 8. Where the field is heading

- **Sites that declare tools:** WebMCP (`document.modelContext`, Chrome origin trial) lets a page hand typed tools to
  an agent. A two-line probe at page load costs nothing and would pay off the day a site offers it.
- **Markdown for agents:** `llms.txt` and `.md` mirrors, which the challenge platform itself serves. Worth probing
  for on unknown sites for the same reason.
- **Code as the action space** is displacing click-by-click loops on long tasks; reported benchmark leads are large.
- **Decision models as cheap policy heads** (Clef): typed, calibrated answers for routing and verification, with a
  generalist model doing the reading.
- **Workflow memory:** agents that keep model-authored routines across runs. Within one run it is allowed here;
  shipping routines learned on public-1 would be pre-solving.
- **Cheaper, faster computer-use models** shrink the gap between pixel and DOM agents; hybrids remain the default
  until they close it.

The plan is written to `docs/architecture-options.md` on the new branch `research/agent-architecture`, uncommitted. Nothing has been built or run yet; this is research and a recommendation only.

## What the challenge actually wants
- **The task:** one signed bid, typed into the tender portal's form and signed with a TAN from the webmail. The answer goes in on the site, not through the API.
- **Ranking:** eligible first (right tender reference in a signed submission), then quality 0–100, then cost × time. Cost and time are only a tie-break.
- **One shot:** exactly one submission ends the run, inside 20 minutes, and the TAN lives 5 minutes.
- **Private final:** it runs our latest passed submission, not our best. Same rules and answer format, but different software, layout, navigation, site names and data, with facts split differently across sites.
- **Review:** an AI reviewer rejects fixed click paths, crawlers and copied values.
- **The field:** the best score on the board is 21.5; most teams are at 0 or ineligible. Our two submissions both scored 0, ineligible.

It is really four problems: finding evidence on hostile sites, deciding which competing record governs, exact arithmetic, and a long stateful form. Browsing frameworks only help with the first and last; most points are lost in the middle two.

## Where the overfit line is
- **Overfit:** selectors, URLs, page labels, click order, branching on site name, prompts that describe the public sites.
- **Underfit:** a generic "browse and figure it out" loop that does arithmetic in its head. This is roughly where the leaderboard is.
- **Target:** hard-code only what the rules guarantee (the 29 rules, the answer schema, the calculator). Leave everything about the sites to the model at run time.

## The option space
The doc lays out five axes with the industry tools on each, then eight named combinations scored on generalisation, quality, time, review risk and effort:
- **What the model sees:** text, accessibility tree, screenshot, marked screenshot, hybrid, network level.
- **How it acts:** click tools, coordinates, natural-language actions, model-written code, HTTP, semantic tools.
- **Who decides:** single loop, planner and executor, lead plus workers, shared ledger, staged graph, voting, verifier, in-run skill learning.
- **Who computes:** the model, or deterministic code fed by typed facts.
- **Which model:** Qwen only, Qwen with Clef as a gate, Qwen with a frontier lead, frontier everywhere.

You are right that a browser-use style loop is not the answer; it is the lowest-ceiling combination. Playwright itself is unavoidable as the transport, because the sandbox only provides browsers over CDP.

## Recommendation
A lead agent plus four site workers (one per browser), run on Qwen with Clef as a cheap yes/no gate:
- **Workers** get questions, never paths, and work out each site's role by looking at it.
- **Shared evidence ledger** holds every finding with its source quote.
- **Deterministic code** picks the governing record (exact reference, authorised sender, latest date not after the scenario date) and does the arithmetic.
- **Verifier** re-checks each fact used against its quote.
- **Generic form filler** enters and signs the bid, starting at a fixed time budget.

Model-written code and a frontier model for the lead come later, and only if test runs show reasoning errors rather than retrieval errors.

Build order: a signed submission with the right reference first, then material and quantity, then price, discount and lead time, then the surcharge, packaging and bonus rules.

To test generalisation with only one public scenario, the doc proposes shuffling and anonymising site ids, rewriting the public pages on the fly, synthetic calculator cases, a lint that fails if any site token appears in `agent/`, and repeat runs to measure variance.

## Things you should know
- **`main` is just the starter kit plus `CLAUDE.md`.** `CLAUDE.md` refers to `docs/plan.md`, `dev/smoke.py` and five harness modules that are not in the repo on any branch. Someone likely has them unpushed.
- **`CLAUDE.md` already records a framework decision** (pydantic-ai on Qwen, no LangGraph, no browser-agent framework). My recommendation is compatible with it.
- **I did not use Chrome.** The platform serves every doc as Markdown, so I fetched those directly. I logged into the scouting sites over plain HTTP with the public scouting logins rather than typing passwords into your browser.
- **Scouting was shallow.** I saw only the landing pages (the ERP returned its flaky 503), and I stopped at the webmail's "not a robot" slider.
- **The `atira` CLI is not installed on this machine**, so I could not check run status or announcements.

One decision for you: do you have a frontier model key the team is willing to use? Without one, the plan stays Qwen plus Clef.

These are the Artifact tool's own rules for the file you publish; the design guidance below builds on them.

Artifacts render mermaid diagrams natively — markdown via ```mermaid fences, HTML via `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks — no library needed, don't load one. Forms work as page UI (inputs, validation, submit events), but a real submission has nowhere to go: handle `submit` in script with `preventDefault()` and never point `action` at another site or a mailto: address. Copy buttons work when `navigator.clipboard.writeText` is called inside the click handler — catch its rejection (older desktop apps and some app views refuse it) and fall back to selecting the text; reading the clipboard never works, though the viewer's own Paste (the `paste` event) does. ```css
:root { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: … }  /* every token, light values */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark } }

It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. **Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. A bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside that padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets this padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.


[Design systems left out, as this call asked: nothing about them was listed or read. If the user or the session named one, read it with its own call.]

Sections
